text: Table 2 shows that, on ordered electricity data, improving coverage through calibration weighting need not require wider intervals once fitting also changes. At a 90% target, ordinary full conformal with least squares (CP+LS) averages 85.2% coverage and width 0.565. Adding weighted least-squares fitting (NexCP+WLS) retains higher coverage, 89.3%, while reducing width to 0.527, below both alternatives; neither weighted method reaches 90% on average. The fitting change thus offers no width advantage in this control, and weighted procedures have greater variability. This contrast supports distinct calibration and fitting benefits in the ordered setting, not a generally narrower weighted method. These averages across prediction times neither establish coverage at every time nor universal 90% coverage under drift, because the theorem's weighted swapped-residual total-variation penalty may be large.

text: Full conformal prediction usually relies on exchangeable data and symmetric fitting, excluding order-sensitive predictors and leaving coverage vulnerable to drift. Our extension separates two roles: fixed calibration weights in [0,1] emphasize observations expected to resemble the test point, while fixed algorithm tags encode information used by nonsymmetric fitting. A data-independent weighted random swap moves the candidate test point to a sampled position before fitting, with tags retained at their positions. This makes miscoverage imply membership in a high-residual set with weighted mass at most alpha. Comparing swapped and original residual-vector distributions yields finite-sample coverage at least 1 - alpha minus their weighted total-variation discrepancy. Under exchangeability this discrepancy vanishes even with nonsymmetric fitting; otherwise, a small discrepancy bounds undercoverage, not exact nominal validity. With distinct residuals, small discrepancy and normalized test weight also limit overcoverage; related bounds extend to split conformal and jackknife+. Simulations and electricity data distinguish calibration gains from width gains: on ordered electricity data, residual weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas adding weighted fitting gives 89.3% coverage and narrower intervals than unweighted fitting, against a 90% target. Permutation removes the width advantage, and election-data coverage also remains below target.
